newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Two-month disarmament of Guatemala rebels begins.
newsitem.headline: Two-month disarmament of Guatemala rebels begins.

text.p: Guatemala's guerrilla forces began handing in their weapons on Monday, effectively ending Central America's longest civil war.
U.N. observers began registering hundreds of former combatants of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), who will spend the next two months in camps where they will turn in weapons.
The leftist rebels fought against a series of military regimes and continued their fight when civilian rule was re-established in the 1980s. A historic peace agreement was signed last December.

"The gathering of former URNG combatants officially begins today, ending the internal armed conflict," guerrilla leader Jorge Soto, who fought under the name Commander Pablo Monsanto, said at a ceremony.
"The URNG is showing its willingness to comply with all the promises it assumed in the peace accords," he said.
Soto joined U.N. and government representatives at official acts marking the beginning of disarmament in Elvira Camp, 60 miles (100 km) from Guatemala City.

A mission of 155 unarmed U.N. observers, the so-called "blue berets," will register the ex-combatants, give them medical exams and verify the turning in of arms in eight different camps in six rural areas around the country.

Soto told reporters the URNG will turn in all their guns and reveal the location of weapons caches to the United Nations under terms of a Dec. 29 peace agreement between the Guatemalan government and the URNG.
Neither Monsanto nor the chief of the U.N. observers, Gen. Jose Rodriguez, would say exactly how many guerrillas will go to the camps nor how many arms would be turned in.
The Guatemala City newspaper Siglo Veintiuno quoted army sources as saying some 3,600 guerrillas will turn in 1,818 weapons and 409 mines.
Rebel disarmament is one aspect of 11 complex and comprehensive accords in December's historic peace agreement.

Under the accords the Guatemalan army, which earned a reputation for rampant human rights violations during 36 years of counterinsurgency campaigns, will shrink by one-third and abandon its state police role.
